reach.e: From Middle English rechen, from Old English rǣċan (“to reach”), from Proto-West Germanic *raikijan, from Proto-Germanic *raikijaną, from the Proto-Indo-European *Hreyǵ- (“to bind, reach”).
reach.g: To extend, stretch, or thrust out (for example a limb or object held in the hand).

reach.e: From Japanese 立直 (rīchi), from Chinese 立直 (lìzhí).

reaching.e: From Middle English reching, rechyng, recchinge, rechand, from Old English *rǣċende and reċċende (“reaching”), from Proto-Germanic *raikijandz, present participle of *raikijaną (“to stretch, reach”) and Proto-Germanic *rakjandz, present participle of *rakjaną (“to stretch, straighten”). Equivalent to reach + -ing.

read.e: From Middle English redde (simple past), red, rad (past participle), from Old English rǣdde (simple past), (ġe)rǣded (past participle), conjugations of rǣdan (“to read”); see above.

reader.e: From Middle English reder, redar, redere, redare, from Old English rēdere, rǣdere (“a reader; scholar; diviner”), from Proto-West Germanic *rādāri, equivalent to read + -er.

readily.e: From Middle English redily, rediliche. By surface analysis, read(i) + -ly.
readily.g: Without unwillingness or hesitation; showing readiness.

reading.e: From Middle English reding, redyng, redand, from Old English rǣdende, present participle of rǣdan (“to read”), equivalent to read + -ing.

ready.e: From Middle English redy, redi, rædiȝ, iredi, ȝerǣdi, alteration ( + -y) of earlier irēd, irede, ȝerād (“ready, prepared”), from Old English rǣde, ġerǣde (also ġerȳde) ("prepared, prompt, ready, ready for riding (horse), mounted (on a horse), skilled, simple, easy"), from Proto-Germanic *garaidijaz, *raidijaz, from base *raidaz (“ready”).
ready.g: Prepared for immediate action or use.

real.e: From Middle English real, from Old French reel, from Late Latin reālis (“actual”), from Latin rēs (“matter, thing”), from Proto-Indo-European *reh₁ís (“wealth, goods”). In modern times, likely strengthened by or conflated with the use of the prefix re-, analyzable as re- + -al.
real.g: True, genuine, not merely nominal or apparent.

real.e: Borrowed from Spanish real (“royal”), from Latin rēgālis (“regal, royal”).
real.g: Former unit of currency of Spain and Spain's colonies.

reality.e: From French réalité (“quality of being real”), from Middle French realité (“property, possession”), from Medieval Latin reālitās, from Late Latin reālis (“real”), equivalent to real + -ity. Recorded since 1550 as a legal term in the sense of “fixed property” (compare real estate, realty); the sense “real existence” is attested from 1647.
reality.g: The state of being actual or real; realness.

realize.e: From real (adjective) + -ize (suffix denoting the making of what is indicated by the word it is attached to), possibly modelled after French réaliser, Middle French réaliser (“to make real; to convert (something) into assets or cash”), from real (“actual, real”) + -iser (suffix denoting the making of what is indicated by the word it is attached to).
realize.g: To become aware of, understand, or appreciate (a fact or situation, especially something which has been true for some time).

really.e: From Middle English really, realy, rialliche, equivalent to real + -ly.
really.g: In a way or manner that is real, not unreal.

realm.e: From Middle English rewme, realme, reaume, from Old French reaume, realme, reialme (“kingdom”), of unclear origins. A postulated *rēgālimen (“domain, kingdom”), Late Latin or Vulgar Latin cross of regimen with rēgālis is usually cited. The modern spelling predominates from around 1600.
realm.g: A territory or state, as ruled by an absolute authority, especially by a king; a kingdom.

reap.e: From Middle English repen, from Old English rēopan, rēpan, variants of Old English rīpan (“to reap”), from Proto-West Germanic *rīpan, from Proto-Germanic *rīpaną (compare West Frisian repe, Norwegian ripa (“to score, scratch”)), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁reyb- (“to snatch”).
reap.g: To cut (for example a grain) with a sickle, scythe, or reaping machine.

reaper.e: From Middle English reper, repare, repere, *riper (the last, attested only in surnames Ryper, Riper, etc.), from Old English rīpere (“reaper”), equivalent to reap + -er.
reaper.g: One who reaps; a person employed to harvest crops from the fields by reaping.

rear.e: From Middle English reren (“to raise”), from Old English rǣran (“to raise, set upright, promote, exalt, begin, create, give rise to, excite, rouse, arouse, stir up”), from Proto-West Germanic *raiʀijan, from Proto-Germanic *raizijaną, *raisijaną (“to cause to rise, raise”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rey- (“to lift oneself, rise”).
rear.g: To bring up to maturity, as offspring; to educate; to instruct; to foster.

rear.e: From Middle English reren, from Old English hrēran (“to move, shake, agitate”), from Proto-Germanic *hrōzijaną (“to stir”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱroHs- (“to mix, stir, cook”).

reason.e: From Middle English resoun, reson, from Anglo-Norman raisun (Old French raison), from Latin ratiō, from ratus, past participle of reor (“reckon”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂reh₁- (“to think”), reanalysed root of *h₂er- (“to put together”).

From Middle English reason, reson, resen, rasen, from Old English ræsn (“beam, rafter, ceiling, wall panel”), probably from Proto-West Germanic *raʀn (“house”), from Proto-Germanic *razną (“house, dwelling”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁erh₁- (“to rest”).

reasonable.e: From Middle English resonable, from Old French resnable, from Classical Latin ratiōnābilis, from ratiō. By surface analysis, reason + -able.
reasonable.g: Having the faculty of reason; rational, reasoning.

reassure.e: From Old French rasseürer (French rassurer), from re- + asseürer; as if re- + assure.
reassure.g: To assure anew; to restore confidence to; to free from fear or self-doubt.

rebel.e: From Middle English rebel, rebell, from Old French rebelle, from Latin rebellis (“waging war again; insurgent”), from rebellō (“to wage war again, fight back”), from re- (“again, back”) + bellō (“to wage war”).
rebel.g: A person who resists an established authority, often violently.

rebel.e: From Middle English rebellen, from Old French rebeller, from Latin rebellō (“to wage war again, fight back”), from re- (“again, back”) + bellō (“to wage war”).
rebel.g: To resist or become defiant toward an authority.

rebelling.e: From Middle English rebellyng; equivalent to rebel + -ing.
rebelling.g: An act or feeling of rebellion.

rebellion.e: From Middle English rebellioun, rebellion, from Old French rebellion, from Latin rebelliō. Equivalent for rebel + -ion.
rebellion.g: Armed resistance to an established government or ruler.

rebellious.e: From Middle English rebellious; equivalent to rebel + -ious.

rebuke.e: From Middle English rebuken, from Anglo-Norman rebuker (“to beat back, repel”), from re- + Old French *buker, buchier, buschier (“to strike, hack down, chop”), from busche (“wood”), from Vulgar Latin *busca (“wood, grove”), from Frankish *busk (“grove”), from Proto-Germanic *buskaz (“bush”); equivalent to re- + bush.

rebut.e: From Middle English rebutten, rebouten, from Old French reboter, rebuter, rebouter, etc., from re- + boter, buter, bouter (“to butt”). Entered English around 1302-1307.
rebut.g: To drive back or beat back; to repulse.

recall.e: From re- + call, probably modelled on Latin revocāre, French rappeler, English withcall.
recall.g: To withdraw, retract (one's words etc.); to revoke (an order).

recede.e: From Middle English receden, from Middle French receder and its etymon Latin recedere (“to withdraw; to go back”), from re- + cedere (“to go”).
recede.g: To move back; to retreat; to withdraw.

receipt.e: From Middle English receyt, recorded since c. 1386 as "statement of ingredients in a potion or medicine," from Anglo-Norman or Old Northern French receite (“receipt, recipe”) (1304), altered (by influence of receit (“he receives”), from Latin recipit) from Old French recete.
receipt.g: The act of receiving, or the fact of having been received.

receive.e: From Middle English receyven, from Old French receivre, from Latin recipere (“take back, accept, etc.”), from re- (“back”) + capiō (“to take”); see capacious.
receive.g: To be given, sent, or paid something.

receiver.e: From Middle English receyvour, from Anglo-Norman receverre, receivour et al., later also reformed as receive + -er.

recent.g: Having happened a short while ago.

reception.e: From Middle English recepcion, reception, from Middle French reception, from Latin receptiōn- (“the act of receiving; reception”), from recipiō (“receive”), from re- (“back”) + capiō (“to hold”). Equivalent to receive + -tion.

recess.e: Noun sense 5 (“decree or resolution of the diet of the Holy Roman Empire, etc.”) is possibly influenced by Italian recesso and refers to a decree or resolution made just before a meeting ends. The adjective and verb are derived from the noun.
recess.g: A depressed, hollow, or indented space; also, a hole or opening.

recite.e: From Middle English reciten, from Old French reciter, from Latin recitō.
recite.g: To repeat aloud (some passage, poem or other text previously memorized, or in front of one's eyes), often before an audience.

reckless.e: From Middle English rekles, reckeles, rekkeles, (also recheles), from Old English rēcelēas (“reckless, careless, negligent”), equivalent to reck + -less.
reckless.g: Careless or heedless; headstrong or rash.

reckon.e: From Middle English rekenen, from Old English recenian (“to pay; arrange, dispose, reckon”) and ġerecenian (“to explain, recount, relate”); both from Proto-West Germanic *rekanōn (“to count, explain”), from Proto-West Germanic *rekan (“swift, ready, prompt”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵ- (“to make straight or right”).
reckon.g: To count; to enumerate; to number; also, to compute; to calculate.

reckoning.e: Gerund of the verb reckon, from reckon + -ing.
reckoning.g: The action of calculating or estimating something.

reclaim.e: From Middle English reclaymen, recleymen, reclamen, from Anglo-Norman reclamer (noun reclaim and Middle French reclamer (noun reclaim), from Latin reclāmō, reclāmāre. Equivalent to re- + claim.
reclaim.g: To return land to a suitable condition for use.

recline.e: Borrowed from Latin reclīnāre (“to bend back”).
recline.g: To cause to lean back; to bend back.

recognize.e: Borrowed from Middle French reconoistre, from Old French reconoistre, from Latin recognoscere, first attested in the 16th century. Latin had rare recognizare (“to try by jury”).
recognize.g: To match (something or someone which one currently perceives) to a memory of some previous encounter with the same person or thing.

recoil.e: From Old French reculer. Further from Latin re- + cūlus.
recoil.g: A starting or falling back; a rebound; a shrinking.

recommend.e: From Middle English recommenden, from Old French recommender (compare French recommander), from Latin re- + commendāre (“to commend, commit; to recommend”), from con- + mandāre (“commit, intrust, enjoin”), from manus (“hand, handwriting, power”) + dare (“to give; to offer or render”).
recommend.g: To bestow commendation on; to represent favorably; to suggest, endorse or encourage as an appropriate choice.

recommendation.e: From Middle English recommendacioun, from Anglo-Norman recomendacion, from Medieval Latin recommendatio. By surface analysis, recommend + -ation.

recompense.e: From Middle English recompense, borrowed from Old French recompense or Medieval Latin recompensa.
recompense.g: An equivalent returned for anything given, done, or suffered; compensation; reward; amends; requital.

recompense.e: From Middle English recompensen, borrowed from Old French recompenser, from Late Latin recompensare, from Latin re- (“again”) + compensare (“to balance out”).
recompense.g: To reward or repay (someone) for something done, given etc.

reconcile.g: To restore a friendly relationship; to bring back or return to harmony.

reconciliation.e: From Middle English reconciliacioun (“act of reconciling; state of accord or harmony;”), from Anglo-Norman reconciliaciun, reconsiliacion, reconsiliaciun, and Middle French reconciliation, reconsiliacion, reconsiliation (“act of reconciling; result of this act; act of bringing about agreement or harmony.
reconciliation.g: The re-establishment of friendly relations; conciliation, rapprochement.

record.e: From Middle English recorde, borrowed from Old French record, from recorder.
record.g: An item of information put into a temporary or permanent physical medium.

record.e: From Middle English recorden (“to repeat, to report”), borrowed from Old French recorder (“to get by heart”), from Latin recordārī (“remember, call to mind”), from re- (“back, again”) + cor (“heart; mind”).
record.g: To make a record of information.

recorder.e: From Middle English recordour, borrowed from Old French recordour, from Old French recordeor, from Medieval Latin recordātor, from Latin recordor (“call to mind, remember, recollect”), from re- (“back, again”) + cor (“heart; mind”). By surface analysis, record + -er.

recount.e: From Old Northern French and Anglo-Norman recunter, variant of Old French reconter.

recover.e: From Middle English recoveren, rekeveren, from Anglo-Norman recoverer and Old French recovrer, from Latin recuperāre, alternative form of reciperāre.
recover.g: To get back, to regain (a physical thing; in astronomy and navigation, sight of a thing or a signal).

recovering.e: From Middle English recoveryng; equivalent to recover + -ing.
recovering.g: The process or the instance of recovery.

recovery.e: From recover + -y, from Middle English recoveree, from Old French recovree, from recovrer (“recover”).
recovery.g: The act or process of regaining or repossession of something lost.

recruit.g: A supply of anything wasted or exhausted; a reinforcement.

recur.e: Borrowed from Latin recurrō (“to hurry or run back; to return, revert”), from re- (prefix meaning ‘back, backwards’) + currō (“to hasten, hurry; to move, travel; to run”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱers- (“to run”)).
recur.g: Of an event, situation, etc.: to appear or happen again, especially repeatedly.

reddish.e: From Middle English redisch; equivalent to red + -ish.

redeem.e: From Middle English redemen, modified from Old French redimer, from Latin redimō (“release; obviate; atone for”), itself from red- (“back; again”) + emō (“buy; gain, take, procure”).
redeem.g: To recover ownership of something by buying it back.

redeemer.e: From Middle English redemer, redemar, equivalent to redeem + -er.
redeemer.g: One who redeems; one who provides redemption.

redemption.e: From Middle English redempcioun, from Old French redemption, from Latin redemptio.
redemption.g: The act of redeeming or something redeemed.

redness.e: From Middle English reednes, rednesse, from Old English rēadnes (“redness”), equivalent to red + -ness.
redness.g: The state or quality of being red.

redound.e: From Anglo-Norman redunder, Middle French redonder, and their source, Latin redundō, from red- + undō (“surge”), from unda (“a wave”).
redound.g: To swell up (of water, waves etc.); to overflow, to surge (of bodily fluids).

reduce.e: From Middle English reducen, from Old French reduire, from Latin redūcō (“reduce”); from re- (“back”) + dūcō (“lead”).
reduce.g: To bring down the size, quantity, quality, value or intensity of something; to diminish, to lower.

reed.e: From Middle English red, from Old English hrēod, from Proto-West Germanic *hreud (“reed”), of uncertain origin. No cognates in North Germanic languages, but the existence of an otherwise unattested Gothic *𐌷𐍂𐌹𐌿𐌳 (*hriud) was supposed by the brothers Grimm.
reed.g: Any of various types of tall stiff perennial grass-like plants growing together in groups near water.

reed.e: From Middle English reden, from the noun (see above).

reef.e: From earlier riff, from Middle English rif, from Old Norse rif (“rib, reef”), from Proto-Germanic *ribją (“rib, reef”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rebʰ- (“arch, ceiling, cover”). Dutch rif (“reef”), Low German riff, reff (“reef”), German Riff (“reef, ledge”) are also borrowed from Old Norse.
reef.g: A chain or range of rocks, sand, or coral lying at or near the surface of the water.

reef.e: From Middle English reef, from Old Norse rif, Middle Dutch rif, rēve, and/or Middle Low German ref. Possibly a figurative use of the word for “rib” in etymology 1 above, in which case all forms must, again, be borrowings from Old Norse. Alternatively it may be a different word related to Old English rift (“curtain, veil”), ārāfian (“to uncoil, wind off”).
reef.g: A portion of a sail rolled and tied down to lessen the area exposed in a high wind.

reel.e: From Middle English reel, reele, from Old English rēol, hrēol, from Proto-West Germanic *hrehul, from Proto-Germanic *hrehulaz, *hrahilaz, from Proto-Indo-European *krek- (“to weave, beat”).

refer.e: From Middle English referren, from Old French referer, from Latin referre. The noun (used in journalism) is from the verb.
refer.g: To direct the attention of (someone toward something).

refiner.g: One who, or that which, refines.

reflect.e: From Old French reflecter (“to bend back, turn back”), from Latin reflectō (“to reflect”), from re- (“again”) + flectō (“to bend, to curve”).
reflect.g: To bend back (light, etc.) from a surface.

reflection.e: From Middle English refleccion, refleccioun, refleccioune, reflection, from Middle French reflection, reflexion, and its source Late Latin reflexiō, from the participle stem of reflectō. The current spelling is influenced by reflect. Equivalent to reflect + -ion.
reflection.g: The act of reflecting or the state of being reflected.

reform.e: From Middle English reformen, from Old French reformer, from Latin reformo, reformare. As a noun since 1660s, from French réforme.
reform.g: The change of something that is defective, broken, inefficient or otherwise negative, in order to correct or improve it

reformation.e: From Middle English reformacioun, reformation, from Middle French reformation and Latin refōrmātiō, refōrmātiōnis (“reform, change”), from refōrmō (“transform, reshape”), from re- + fōrmō (“shape, form”). By surface analysis, reform + -ation.
reformation.g: An improvement (or an intended improvement) in the existing form or condition of institutions or practices, etc.; intended to make a strikin

reformation.e: Originally a variant of Etymology 1. In later use also independently from re- + formation, after re-form.

refrain.e: From Middle English refreynen, from Anglo-Norman refrener, Old French refrener, from Latin refrēnāre, from re- + frēnāre, from frēnum.
refrain.g: To hold back, to restrain (someone or something).

refrain.e: From French refrain, from the Old French verb refraindre (“to break off, repeat”), from Latin re- (“back, again”) + frangō (“break”); compare Occitan refranhs (“a refrain”), refranher (“to repeat”).
refrain.g: The chorus or burden of a song repeated at the end of each verse or stanza.

refresh.e: From Middle English refreshen, refreschen, refrisschen, from Old French refrescher (“to refresh”) (modern French rafraîchir), equivalent to re- + fresh.

refreshing.g: That refreshes someone; pleasantly fresh and different; granting vitality and energy.

refreshment.e: Recorded since 1665; either directly or via Middle English refreschement, from Old French refrescher (12th century; modern French rafraîchir), itself from re- (“again”) + fresche (“fresh”) (modern French frais; from a Germanic source, cognate with Old High German frisc, modern German frisch, Dutch fris, etc.)
refreshment.g: The process of refreshing; a means of restoring strength, energy or vigour.

refuge.e: From Middle English refuge, from Old French refuge, from Latin refugium, from re- + fugiō (“flee”).
refuge.g: A state of safety, protection or shelter.

refugee.e: From French réfugié, past participle of réfugier (“to take refuge, to seek refuge”), from Old French refuge (“hiding place”) from Latin refugium (“a place of refuge, place to flee back to”), originally describing French Huguenots fleeing religious persecution after the revocation of the Edict of Nantes in 1685.
refugee.g: A person seeking refuge (as for shelter or protection), especially in a foreign country, out of fear or prospect of political, religious per

refuse.e: Borrowed into late Middle English from Middle French refusé, past participle of refuser (“to refuse”).

From Middle English refusen, from Old French refuser, from Vulgar Latin *refūsāre, either from a blend of Classical Latin refūtāre (whence also refute) and recūsāre (whence also recuse) or from Latin refūsus, the perfect passive participle of refundere (“to pour back”, whence also refund).

refute.g: To prove (something) to be false or incorrect.

regain.e: From Middle French regaigner (French regagner). By surface analysis, re- + gain.
regain.g: To get back; to recover possession of.

regard.e: From Middle English regard, regarde, reguard, from Anglo-Norman reguard, from regarder, reguarder. Piecewise doublet of reward; compare also guard, ward, guardian, and so on.
From Middle English regarden, from Old French regarder, reguarder.

regarded.e: Popularized on Reddit beginning around 2022 in response to increasing censorship of the words retard and retarded.

regeneration.e: From re- + generation or regenerate + -ion, from Latin regenerātiō.
regeneration.g: Rebuilding or restructuring; large scale repair or renewal; revitalisation.

regiment.e: From Middle French regement, régiment, and its source, Late Latin regimentum (“direction for government; course of medical treatment”), from Latin regō (“rule”).
regiment.g: A unit of armed troops under the command of an officer, and consisting of several smaller units.

region.e: From Middle English regioun, from Anglo-Norman regiun, from Latin regiō, from regō.
region.g: Any considerable and connected part of a space or surface; specifically, a tract of land or sea of considerable but indefinite extent; a cou

register.e: From Medieval Latin registrum, from Late Latin regesta (“list, items recorded”), from Latin regerō (“to record, to carry back”), from re- + gerō (“to carry, bear”). Some senses influenced by association with unrelated Latin regō (“to rule”).
register.g: A formal recording of names, events, transactions, etc.

regret.e: From Middle English regretten, regreten, from Old French regreter, regrater (“to lament”), from re- (intensive prefix) + *greter, *grater (“to weep”), from Frankish *grātan (“to weep, mourn, lament”), from Proto-Germanic *grētaną (“to weep”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰreh₁d- (“to sound”); and Frankish *greutan (“to cry, weep”).
regret.g: To feel sorry about (a thing that has or has not happened), afterthink: to wish that a thing had not happened, that something else had happe

regroup.e: Borrowed from French regrouper. By surface analysis, re- + group.

regular.e: From Middle English reguler, from Anglo-Norman reguler, Middle French reguler, regulier, and their source, Latin rēgulāris (“continuing rules for guidance”), from rēgula (“rule”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵ- (“move in a straight line”).
regular.g: Bound by religious rule; belonging to a monastic or religious order (often as opposed to secular).

regulate.e: Borrowed from Latin regulatus, perfect passive participle of regulō (“to direct, rule, regulate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from regula (“rule”), from regō (“to keep straight, direct, govern, rule”).

regulation.g: The act of regulating or the condition of being regulated.

rehearse.e: From Middle English rehersen, from Anglo-Norman reherser (“to repeat word-for-word”).
rehearse.g: To repeat, as what has been already said; to tell over again; to recite.

reign.e: From Middle English regnen, from Old French reignier, from the Latin verb rēgnō, and the noun rēgnum.

reins.e: From Old French reins, from Latin rēnes (“kidneys”); see also French rein.

reject.e: From Late Middle English rejecten, from Latin reiectus, past participle of reicere (“to throw back”), from re- (“back”) + iacere (“to throw”).
reject.g: To refuse to accept; to forswear.

rejection.e: From French réjection or directly from Latin reiectiōnem, accusative of Latin reiectiō.

rejoice.e: From Middle English rejoicen, rejoisen, from Old French resjoir. Spanish regocijar; Portuguese regozijar; Italian gioire.
rejoice.g: To be very happy, be delighted, exult; to feel joy.

rejoin.e: From Middle English rejoynen, partly from Middle French rejoin- (stem of rejoindre, from re- (“again”) + joindre (“to join”)) and partly from re- + joynen. By surface analysis, re- + join.
rejoin.g: To join again; to unite after separation.

rejoin.e: From Middle English rejoynen, from Middle French rejoin- (stem of rejoindre, from re- (“again”) + joindre (“to join”)). By surface analysis, re- + join.

relate.e: From Latin relātus, perfect passive participle of referō (“carry back; report”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).
relate.g: To tell in a descriptive way.

relation.e: From Middle English relacion, relacioun, from Anglo-Norman relacioun and Old French relacion (whence French relation), from Latin relātiō, noun of process form from perfect passive participle relātus (“related”), from verb referō (“to refer, to relate”), from prefix re- (“again”) + ferō (“to bear, to carry”). By surface analysis, relate + -ion.
relation.g: The manner in which two things may be associated.

relationship.g: A connection or association; the condition of being related.

relative.e: From Middle French relatif, from Late Latin relātīvus, from Latin relātus, perfect passive participle of referō (“to carry back, to ascribe”), from re- (“again”) + ferō (“to bear or carry”). By surface analysis, relate + -ive.
relative.g: Connected to or depending on something else; comparative.

relay.e: From Middle French relai (“reserve pack of hounds”), from relaier (“to exchange tired animals for fresh”); literally, "to leave behind", from Old French relaier (“to leave behind”), from re- + laier (“to leave”), of uncertain origin.

release.e: From Middle English relesen, relessen, from Old French relaisser (variant of relascher).
release.g: The event of setting (someone or something) free (e.g. hostages, slaves, prisoners, caged animals, hooked or stuck mechanisms).

relent.e: From Middle English relenten, from Anglo-Norman relentir, from Latin re- + lentare (“to bend”), from lentus (“soft, pliant, slow”). Earliest recording dates to 1526.
relent.g: To give in or be swayed; to become less hard, harsh, or cruel; to show clemency.

relief.e: From Old French relief (“assistance”), from Old French relever (“to relieve”), from Latin relevare (“to raise up, make light”).
relief.g: The removal of stress or discomfort.

relief.e: From Italian rilievo, from rilevare (“to raise”), from Latin relevō (“to raise”).
relief.g: A method of sculpture or other artwork in which shapes or figures protrude from a flat background.

relieve.e: From Late Middle English releven, from Old French relever, specifically from the conjugated forms such as (jeo) relieve (“I lift up”), and its source, Latin relevo (“to lift up, lighten, relieve, alleviate”), combined form of re- (“back”) + levo (“to lift”).
relieve.g: To ease (a person, person's thoughts etc.) from mental distress; to stop (someone) feeling anxious or worried, to alleviate the distress of.

religion.e: From Middle English religioun, from Old French religion, from Latin religiō (“scrupulousness, pious misgivings, superstition, conscientiousness, sanctity, an object of veneration, cult-observance, reverence”).
religion.g: Belief in a spiritual or metaphysical reality (often including at least one deity), accompanied by practices or rituals pertaining to the be

religious.e: From Middle English religiouse, religious, religius, religeous, from Anglo-Norman religieus, religius, from Old French religious, religieux, and their source, Latin religiōsus (“religious, superstitious, conscientious”), from religiō.

relinquish.e: From Middle English relinquisshen, from the inflected stem relinquiss- of Middle French relinquir, from Latin relinquere, itself from re- + linquere (“to leave”).
relinquish.g: To give up, abandon or retire from something; to trade away.

rely.e: From Middle English relien, from Old French relier (“fasten, attach, rally, oblige”), from Latin religo (“fasten, bind fast”), from re- + ligo.
rely.g: To trust; to have confidence in.

remain.e: From Middle English remainen, from Old French remain-, stressed stem of remanoir, from Latin remaneō, maneō, from Proto-Indo-European *men- (“to stay”).
remain.g: That which is left; relic; remainder.

remainder.e: From Middle English remaindre, remeigner, from Anglo-Norman remaindre, with infinitive used as noun.
remainder.g: A part or parts remaining after some has/have been removed or already occurred.

remaining.g: An act or occurrence by which someone or something remains

remark.e: From Middle French remarquer, from Old French remarquer, from re- (“again”) + marquer (“to mark”), equivalent to re- (“again”) + mark.
remark.g: An act of pointing out or noticing; notice or observation.

remedy.e: From Middle English remedie, from Old French *remedie, remede, from Latin remedium (“a remedy, cure”), from re- (“again”) + mederi (“to heal”).

remember.e: From Middle English remembren, from Old French remembrer (“to remember”), from Late Latin rememorari (“to remember again”), from re- + memor (“mindful”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)mer- (“to think about, be mindful, remember”). Middle English minnen (“to remember, have in mind”), from Old Norse minna (“to remind”).
remember.g: To recall from one's memory; to have an image in one's memory.

remembrance.e: From Middle English remembraunce, from Old French remembrance, from remembrer (“to remember”), from Late Latin rememorārī (“to call to mind, to remember”). Equivalent to remember + -ance.
remembrance.g: The act of remembering; a holding in mind, or bringing to mind; recollection.

remind.e: From mid 17th century, equivalent to re- + mind (“to remember”). Probably suggested by obsolete rememorate with the same sense.
remind.g: To cause one to experience a memory (of someone or something); to bring to the notice or consideration (of a person).

remiss.e: From Middle English remisse, remysse, from Latin remissus (“languid, negligent”), perfect passive participle of remittō (“remit”).
remiss.g: At fault; failing to fulfill responsibility, duty, or obligations.

remission.e: From Middle English remissioun (“release from duty; freeing of captives; mercy, pardon, respite; forgiveness; release from or reduction of penances; reduction in intensity (of a quality, symptom, etc.); transfer of property, quitclaim; legal opinion or submission; reference, cross-reference”).
remission.g: A pardon of a sin; (chiefly historical, also figuratively) the forgiveness of an offence, or relinquishment of a (legal) claim or a debt.
To change the mission of; to provide with a new mission.

remit.e: From Middle English remitten, from Latin remittere (“to send, send back”).
remit.g: To transmit or send (e.g. money in payment); to supply.

remnant.e: From Middle English, contraction of remenant, from Anglo-Norman remanant, present participle of remaindre, from Latin remaneō.
remnant.g: A small portion remaining of a larger thing or group; part of a former whole.

remote.e: From Middle English remote, from Old French remot, masculine, remote, feminine, from Latin remotus, past participle of removere (“to remove”), from re- + movere (“to move”).

remove.e: From Middle English removen, from Anglo-Norman remover, removeir, from Old French remouvoir, from Latin removēre, from re- + movēre (“to move”), equivalent to re- + move.

rend.e: From Middle English renden, from Old English rendan (“to rend, tear, cut, lacerate, cut down”), from Proto-West Germanic *(h)randijan (“to tear”), of uncertain origin. Believed by some to be the causative of Proto-Germanic *hrindaną (“to push”).
rend.g: To separate into parts with force or sudden violence; to split; to burst.

render.e: From Middle English renderen, rendren, from Old French rendre (“render, give back”), from Late Latin rendere, from Latin reddere (“make, give back”).

renew.e: From Middle English renewen, an alteration (possibly on analogy with Latin renovāre) of earlier anewen (“to renew”), from Old English nīewian (“to restore; renovate; renew”), equivalent to re- + new.
renew.g: To make (something) new again; to restore to freshness or original condition.

renounce.e: From Old French renoncier (French renoncer), from Latin renūntiō.

renown.e: From Old French renoun (compare with Modern French renom), equivalent to re- + noun.

rent.e: From Middle English rent, rente, from Old French rente, from Early Medieval Latin rendita, from Late Latin rendere, from Latin reddere.
rent.g: A payment made by a tenant at intervals in order to lease a property.

repair.e: Coined between 1300 and 1350 from Middle English repairen, from Middle French reparer, from Latin reparō (“renew, repair”).
repair.g: To restore to good working order, fix, or improve damaged condition; to mend; to remedy.

repair.e: From Middle English repairen (“to return”), from Old French repairier, from Late Latin repatriare (“to return to one's country”), from re- + patria (“homeland”).
repair.g: The act of repairing or resorting to a place.

repay.e: From Old French repaier (“to pay back”), from re- + paiier (“to pay”), from Latin pācāre (“to settle, to make peaceful”), from pāx (“peace”) + -ō (forming verbs). Equivalent to re- + pay.
repay.g: Synonym of pay back in all senses.

repayment.e: From repay + -ment, also equivalent to re- + payment.

repeal.e: From Anglo-Norman repeler, from Old French rapeler (“to call back, call in, call after, revoke”), from Latin repellō (“drive or thrust back”), from re- and pellō (“push or strike”).

repeat.e: From Middle English repeten, from Old French repeter, from Latin repetō, from the prefix re- (“again”) + petō (“to attack, beseech”).
repeat.g: To do or say again (and again).

repel.e: From Middle English repellen, a borrowing from Old French *repeller, from Latin repellere (“to drive back”), from re- (“back”) + pellere (“to drive”).
repel.g: To turn (someone) away from a privilege, right, job, etc.

repent.e: From Middle English repenten, from Old French repentir, from Vulgar Latin *repaenitīre, from Late Latin paenitīre, from Classical Latin paenitēre.
repent.g: To feel pain, sorrow, or regret for what one has done or omitted to do; the cause for repenting may be indicated with "of".

repent.e: From Latin rēpēns, present participle of rēpō (“to creep”).

repentance.g: The action of repenting, an instance of it, atonement.

repentant.e: From Middle English repentant, from Old French repentant, present participle of repentir. By surface analysis, repent + -ant.
repentant.g: Feeling or showing sorrow for wrongdoing.

repetition.e: Borrowed from Latin repetitionem (accusative singular of repetitio; cf. French répétition). By surface analysis, repeat + -ition.
repetition.g: The act or an instance of repeating or being repeated.

replenish.e: From Middle English replenisshen, borrowed from Old French repleniss-, stem of some of the conjugated forms of replenir, from re- + plenir, from plein, from Latin plenus.
replenish.g: To refill; to renew; to supply again or to add a fresh quantity to.

replica.e: Borrowed from Italian replica, derived from Latin replicare (“to fold or bend back; to reply”).

reply.e: From Middle English replyen, replien, borrowed from Old French replier (“to reply”), from the Latin replicō, replicāre (“to fold back”) (in Late or Medieval Latin "to reply, repeat"), from re + plicō (“to fold”); the noun derives from the verb by nominalisation.
reply.g: To give a written or spoken response, especially to a question, request, accusation or criticism; to answer.

report.e: From Middle English reporten, from Anglo-Norman reporter, from Latin reportāre (“to carry back, return, remit, refer”), from re- + portāre.
report.g: To relate details of (an event or incident); to recount, describe (something).

repose.e: Noun etymology 1, noun sense 12.3 (“technique of including in a painting an area or areas which are dark, indistinct, or soft in tone”) is borrowed from French repos.
repose.g: To lay (someone, or part of their body) down to rest.

repose.e: From Middle English reposen (“to put (something) back, replace”), from re- (prefix meaning ‘again; back, backwards’) + posen (“to place (something)”), modelled after Latin repōnō (“to put back; to restore; to store”). Posen is derived from Old French poser (“to place, put”) (modern French poser), from Vulgar Latin pausāre.
repose.g: Senses relating to placing or positioning.

represent.e: From Old French représenter, from Latin repraesentō.
represent.g: To present again or anew; to present by means of something standing in the place of; to exhibit the counterpart or image of; to typify.

representation.e: From Late Middle English representacioun, from Old French representacion, from Latin repraesentātiō. By surface analysis, represent + -ation.

representative.e: From Middle English representative, from Middle French representatif and its etymon Medieval Latin repraesentātīvus. By surface analysis, represent + -ative;.
representative.g: Typical; having the same properties or interest as a larger group.

reprimand.e: From French réprimande, from réprimer (“to repress”).
reprimand.g: A severe, formal or official reproof; reprehension, rebuke, private or public.

reproach.e: From Middle English reprochen, from Old French reprochier (Modern French reprocher).
reproach.g: A mild rebuke, or an implied criticism.

reproof.e: From Old French reprove, from reprover.
reproof.g: An act or instance of reproving or of reprobating; a rebuke, a reproach, an admonition.

reprove.e: From Middle English repreven, reproven, from Anglo-Norman reprover, Middle French reprouver, from Latin reprobāre.

reptile.e: From Middle English reptil, from Old French reptile, from Late Latin rēptile, neuter of reptilis (“creeping”), from Latin rēpō (“to creep”), from Proto-Indo-European *rep- (“to creep, slink”) (Pokorny; Watkins, 1969).
reptile.g: A (typically scaly and egg-laying) cold-blooded vertebrate tetrapod animal, of the class Reptilia (excluding birds), such as a lizard, turtl

repulsive.e: Borrowed from Middle French repulsif, from Medieval Latin repulsivus, from Latin repulsus. By surface analysis, repuls(e) + -ive.
repulsive.g: Tending to rouse aversion or to repulse; disgusting.

reputation.e: 14c. "credit, good reputation", from Middle English reputacion, reputacioun, reputation, reputatioun, from Anglo-Norman reputacion, reputacioun, Middle French reputation (French réputation), and their etymon Latin reputātiōnem (“consideration, thinking over”), noun of action from past participle stem of reputō (“reflect upon, reckon, count over”).
reputation.g: What somebody or something is known for.

repute.e: From Old French reputer, from Latin reputō (“to count over, reckon, calculate, compute, think over, consider”), from re- (“again”) + putō (“to think”).

request.e: From Middle English request, from Old French requeste (French requête), from Vulgar Latin *requaesita, from Latin requīsīta, feminine of requīsītus (“requested, demanded”), past participle of requīrō (“require, ask”), composed of re- + quaerō (“to seek, look for”), of uncertain origin, but possibly from Proto-Italic *kʷaizeō.

require.e: From Old French requerre (whence Modern French requérir), from Latin requīrō (“to require, seek, ask for”, literally “to seek back”), from re- (“back; again”) + quaerō (“to seek”, whence query).
require.g: To demand, to insist upon (having); to call for authoritatively.

requite.e: Quitte is derived from Latin quiētus (“at rest; quiet”), the perfect passive participle of quiēscō (“to repose, rest; to sleep; to be quiet or still”), from quiēs (“rest, repose; sleep; calm, peace, quiet”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷyeh₁- (“to rest; peace, rest”)) + -scō (suffix forming verbs with the sense ‘to begin to do’).
requite.g: To repay (a debt owed); specifically, to recompense or reward someone for (a favour, a service rendered, etc.)

rereward.g: Obsolete spelling of rearward (in the archaic and historical military sense of rearguard and the obsolete sense of haunches, buttocks) .

rescue.e: From Middle English rescouen, from Old French rescoure, rescurre, rescorre; from Latin prefix re- (“re-”) + excutere (“to shake or drive out”), from ex (“out”) + quatiō (“to shake”).
rescue.g: To save from any violence, danger or evil.

rescuer.g: A person who rescues someone or something.

resemblance.e: From Anglo-Norman resemblance, from Old French (compare French ressemblance). Morphologically resemble + -ance.
resemblance.g: The quality or state of resembling.

resemble.e: From Middle English resemblen, from Anglo-Norman resembler, ressembler, from re- + sembler (“to seem”). By surface analysis, re- + semble.
resemble.g: To be like or similar to (something); to represent as similar.

resent.e: From Middle French ressentir, resentir, from Old French resentir (Modern ressentir), from re- + sentir (“to feel”).
resent.g: To feel resentment over; to consider as an affront.

resentment.e: From resent + -ment, after Middle French and French ressentiment (in Old French as recentement), from an archaic usage of the verb ressentir via Old French sentir, from Latin sentiō, sentīre (“to feel”).
resentment.g: Anger or displeasure stemming from belief that one or one's group has been wronged or betrayed by others; indignation.

reserve.e: From Old French reserver, from Latin reservō (“to reserve, retain”).

reservoir.e: From French réservoir (“collection place”) (fig.), réservoir (“storehouse”) (lit.). in turn from French réserver (“to reserve, keep”).
reservoir.g: A place where anything is kept in store.

reside.e: From Middle English residen, from Old French resider, from Latin resideō (“remain behind, reside, dwell”), from re- (“back”) + sedeō (“sit”).
reside.g: To dwell permanently or for a considerable time; to have a settled abode for a time; to remain for a long time.

residence.e: From Middle English residence, from Old French residence, from Medieval Latin residentia, from residēns, present participle of resideō, equivalent to reside + -ence.
residence.g: The place where one lives (resides); one's home.

resident.e: From Middle English resident, from Anglo-Norman resident, from Latin residēns, present participle of resideō (“to remain behind, reside, dwell”), equivalent to reside + -ent, from re- (“back”) + sedeō (“to sit”). The espionage sense is a semantic loan from Russian резиде́нт (rezidént).
resident.g: A person, animal or plant living at a certain location or in a certain area.

residue.e: From Middle English residue, from Old French residu, from Latin residuum, neuter of residuus (“remaining”), from resideō (“to remain behind”).
residue.g: That which persists or remains following the removal or elimination of other elements.

resin.e: From Middle English resyn, resyne, from Old French résine, from Latin resīna.
resin.g: A viscous water-insoluble hydrocarbon exudate of certain plants, or such a substance as a component of a plant exudate; used in lacquers, va

resist.e: From Middle English resisten, from Middle French resister and Old French resistre, and their source, Latin resistere, from re- + sistere (“cause to stand”).
resist.g: To attempt to counter the actions or effects of.

resistance.e: From earlier resistence, from Middle English resistence, from Old French resistence, from Latin resistentia. Morphologically resist + -ance.
resistance.g: The act of resisting, or the capacity to resist.

resolution.e: Recorded since 1412, as Middle English resolucioun (“dissolution”), either from Anglo-Norman resolucion or directly from Latin resolūtiō (“a loosening, solution”), from resolvō (“to loosen”), itself from the intensive prefix re- + solvō (“to loosen”). By surface analysis, recognizably related to resolve and -tion.
resolution.g: A firm decision or an official decision.

resolve.e: From Middle English resolven, from Old French resolver, a learned borrowing of Latin resolvō (“loosen, thaw, melt, resolve”), equivalent to re- + solve. Piecewise doublet of re-solve.
resolve.g: To find a solution to (a problem).

resort.e: From Middle English resorten, from Old French resortir (“to fall back, return, resort, have recourse, appeal”), back-formation from sortir (“to go out”).
resort.g: A place where people go for recreation, especially one with facilities such as lodgings, entertainment, and a relaxing environment.

resound.e: From both of the following: From Late Middle English resounen (“to return with an echo, resound; to make a sound, to sound; of speech or writing: to announce a theme”), from Anglo-Norman resoner, resouner, Middle French resoner, and Old French resoner (“to make a (deep or echoing) sound; of sounds: to echo; to ring.
resound.g: To make (sounds), or to speak (words), loudly or reverberatingly.

resound.e: From Late Middle English resoun, reson (“echoing or reverberating sound; clangour, din, noise”), from Old French reson, and from its etymon Latin resonus (“echoing, resounding”), from re- (prefix meaning ‘again’) + sonus (“sound; noise; pitch; speech; (figuratively) character, style, tone.
resound.g: An echoing or reverberating sound; a resounding.

resounding.g: Having a deep, rich sound; mellow and resonant.

resource.e: Borrowed from Middle French ressource, from Old French resourse, resource (“a source, spring”), from resourdre, from Latin resurgō (“to rise again, spring up anew”). Equivalent to re- + source.
resource.g: Something that one uses to achieve an objective, e.g. raw materials or personnel.

respect.e: From Middle English respect, from Old French respect, also respit (“respect, regard, consideration”), from Latin respectus (“a looking at, regard, respect”), perfect passive participle of respiciō (“look at, look back upon, respect”), from re- (“back”) + speciō (“to see”), equivalent to re- + -spect.
respect.g: An attitude of consideration or high regard; a feeling of admiration or esteem.

respite.e: From Anglo-Norman and Old French respit (“rest”), from Latin respectus.
respite.g: A brief interval of rest or relief.

resplendent.e: From the obsolete sense of the English verb splendish (“to shine”), from Latin splendere (“to shine”), or from resplend + -ent, from Latin resplendere (“to shine back, glitter”).

respond.e: From Middle English respounden, from Old French respondre, from Late Latin respondō, from Latin respondeō. Modern French répondre.
respond.g: To say something in return; to answer; to reply.

response.e: From Middle English respounse, respons, from Old French respons, respuns, responce, ultimately from the Latin respōnsum, a nominal use of the neuter form of respōnsus, the perfect passive participle of respondeō, from re (“again”) + spondeō (“promise”).
response.g: An answer or reply, or something in the nature of an answer or reply.

responsibility.e: From responsible + -ity. Although the components are of French origin, the compound appears to have been formed in English. Later-attested French responsabilité is modeled on the English word, and Italian responsabilità is in turn modeled on the French.
responsibility.g: The state of being responsible, accountable, or answerable.

responsible.e: From Middle French responsable, from Old French responsable, responsible, formed from the root of Latin responsus, from respondeō, respondēre. The spelling of the English word is taken from the Old French variant responsible. By surface analysis, response + -ible.
responsible.g: Having the duty of taking care of something; answerable for an act performed or for its consequences; accountable; amenable, especially lega

rest.e: From Middle English rest, reste, from Old English ræst, from Proto-West Germanic *rastu, from Proto-Germanic *rastō, of uncertain origin; possibly derived from Proto-Indo-European *h₁reh₁- (“to rest”) or *Hre(h₁)s- (“to flow, rush”).
rest.g: Relief from work or activity by sleeping; sleep.

rest.e: From Middle English resten, from Old French rester, from Latin restō.
rest.g: To continue to be, remain, be left in a certain way.

restitution.e: From Old French restitucion, from Latin restitutio. By surface analysis, restitute + -ion.
restitution.g: A process of compensation for losses.

restless.e: From Middle English restles, restelees, from Old English ræstlēas, equivalent to rest + -less.

restoration.e: From Middle English restoracion, altered from restauracion (from Latin restaurātiō) by partly deriving from restoren + -acion. By surface analysis, restore + -ation.
restoration.g: The process of bringing an object back to its original state; the process of restoring something.

restore.e: From Middle English restoren, from Old French restorer, from Latin rēstaurāre. By surface analysis, re- + store.
restore.g: To reestablish, or bring back into existence.

restrain.e: From Middle English restreinen, from Old French restreindre, from Latin rēstringere (“fasten, tighten”).
restrain.g: To control or keep in check.

restraint.e: From Middle English restreynte, from Old French restreinte; more at restrain.
restraint.g: Something that restrains, ties, fastens or secures.

restrict.e: Borrowed from Latin restrictus, perfect passive participle of restringō (“draw back tightly; restrain, restrict”), from re- (“back, again”) + stringō (“press, tighten, compress”).
restrict.g: To restrain within boundaries; to limit; to confine

restriction.e: From Middle English restriccioun, from Anglo-Norman restriction, Middle French restriction, and their source, Late Latin restrictiō, from Latin restringō. Morphologically restrict + -ion.
restriction.g: The act of restricting, or the state of being restricted.

result.e: Recorded since 1432 as Middle English resulten, from Medieval Latin resultare, in Classical Latin "to spring forward, rebound", the frequentative of the past participle of resilio (“to rebound”), from re- (“back”) + salio (“to jump, leap”).
result.g: To proceed, spring up or rise, as a consequence, from facts, arguments, premises, combination of circumstances, consultation, thought or end

resume.e: From Anglo-Norman resumer, Middle French resumer, from Latin resumere, from re- + sumere (“to take”).
Borrowed from French résumé, past participle of résumer (“to summarize”), from Latin resūmere (“to take back”); compare resume.

resurrection.e: From Middle English resurreccioun, resurrection, from Anglo-Norman resurrectiun, Old French resurrection (French: résurrection), and their etymon Late Latin resurrēctiōnem (accusative of resurrēctiō) from Latin resurgō (“to rise again”), from re- (“again”), + surgō (“to rise”). By surface analysis, resurrect + -ion.
resurrection.g: The act of arising from the dead and becoming alive again.

retain.e: From Late Middle English reteinen, retein (“to continue to keep, retain; to continue to possess; to possess; to contain; to draw back, retire; to hold back, restrain; to keep in mind, remember; to take back, repossess; to appoint; to engage in one’s service, employ, hire”).
retain.g: Often followed by from: to hold back (someone or something); to check, to prevent, to restrain, to stop.

retain.e: Partly: from Middle English retein, retain (“possession of a sum of money”); and from the verb (see etymology 1).
retain.g: An act of holding or keeping something; a possession, a retention.

retaliate.e: From Latin retāliātus, past participle of retāliō (“to requite, retaliate”).
retaliate.g: To do something harmful or negative to get revenge for some harm; to fight back or respond in kind to an injury or affront.

retire.e: From Middle French retirer (“draw back”), from Old French retirer, built from re- (“back”) + tirer (“draw, pull”), the latter from Vulgar Latin *tīrāre, of highly uncertain origin.
retire.g: To stop working on a permanent basis, usually because of old age or illness.

retort.e: From Middle English retorte, from Latin retortus, from retorquēre (“to be forced to twist back”).
retort.g: A sharp or witty reply, or one which turns an argument against its originator; a comeback.
A flask with a rounded base and a long neck that is bent down and tapered, used to heat a liquid for distillation.

retreat.e: From Middle English retret, from Old French retrait or retret, from Latin retractus, from retraho.
retreat.g: The act of pulling back or withdrawing, as from something dangerous, or unpleasant.

retribution.g: Punishment inflicted in the spirit of moral outrage or personal vengeance.

retrieve.e: Recorded in Middle English c. 1410 as retreve (altered to retrive in the 16th century; modern form is from c. 1650), from Middle French retruev-, stem of Old French retrover (“to find again”, modern retrouver), itself from re- (“again”) + trover (“to find”), probably from Vulgar Latin *tropāre (“to compose”).
retrieve.g: To regain or get back something.

return.e: From Middle English returnen, retornen, from Anglo-Norman returner, from Old French retourner, retorner, from Medieval Latin retornare (“to turn back”), from re- + tornare (“to turn”). By surface analysis, re- + turn.
return.g: To come or go back (to a place or person).

reveal.e: From Middle English revēlen, from Old French reveler, from Latin revēlāre (“to reveal, uncover”), from re- (“back, again”) + vēlāre (“to cover”).
reveal.g: The outer side of a window or door frame.

revealer.e: From Middle English revelare, equivalent to reveal + -er.
revealer.g: A person or thing that reveals.

revealing.e: From Middle English reveling; equivalent to reveal + -ing.

revel.e: From Middle English revelen, from Old French revel, from reveler (“to be disorderly, to make merry”), from Latin rebello (“to rebel”).
revel.g: An instance of merrymaking; a celebration.

revel.e: From Latin revellere, from re- + vellere (“to pluck, pull”).

revelation.e: From Middle English revelacioun, from Old French revelacion, from Latin revēlātiō (“disclosure”), from revēlō (“to disclose”), re (“again”) + vēlō (“to cover”); by surface analysis, revelate + -ion.
revelation.g: The act of revealing or disclosing.

reveling.e: From Middle English revelynge; equivalent to revel + -ing.

revelry.e: From Middle English revelrye; equivalent to revel + -ry.

revenge.e: From Middle French revenge, a derivation from revenger, from Old French revengier (possibly influenced by Old Occitan revènge (“revenge, comeback”), from Old Occitan revenir (“to come back”)), a variant of Middle French revancher (whence deverbal French revanche), from Old French revenchier.
revenge.g: Any form of personal, retaliatory action against an individual, institution, or group for some alleged or perceived harm or injustice.

revenge.e: From Middle English revengen, from Old French revengier, revenger.
revenge.g: To take revenge for (a particular harmful action) or on behalf of (its victim); to avenge.

revenue.e: Recorded in English from 1433, "income from property or possessions", from Middle French revenue, from Old French (“a return”) (modern French revenu), the prop. feminine past participle of revenir (“come back”) (=modern French), from Latin revenire (“to return, come back”), from re- (“back”) + venire (“to come”).
revenue.g: The income returned by an investment.

reverberate.e: Borrowed from Latin reverberātus, perfect passive participle of reverberō (“to rebound; to reflect; to repel”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), whence Middle French reverberer (French réverbérer) and Middle English reverberen (“to send back”)), from re- (prefix meaning ‘again’) and verberō (“to beat; to lash, whip”) (from verber (“rod.
reverberate.g: To cause (a sound) to be (repeatedly) bounced against one or more surfaces; to re-echo.

reverberate.e: Borrowed from Latin reverberātus, see Etymology 1 and -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more. etymology 2, adjective sense 2 (“ringing or vibrating with many echoing sounds”) was popularized by its use in Twelfth Night (written c. 1601–1602; published 1623) by the English playwright William Shakespeare (1564–1616): see the quotation.
reverberate.g: Synonym of reverberant (“that tends to reverberate (“(repeatedly) bounce against one or more surfaces”) or has reverberated”); re-echoed.

revere.e: Borrowed from French révérer, ultimately from Latin revereor, from re- + vereor (“to fear”).
revere.g: To regard someone or something with great awe or devotion.

reverence.e: From Middle English reverence (noun) and reverencen (verb), from Old French reverence and Latin reverentia, from Latin revereor (“to stand in awe, respect, revere”), from re- + vereor, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to cover, heed, notice”).
reverence.g: Veneration; profound awe and respect, normally in a sacred context.

reverend.e: Borrowed from Middle French révérend, from Old French, from Latin future passive participle reverendus (“that is to be respected”), from deponent verb revereor (“to honor, revere”).

reverent.e: From Middle English reverent, from Middle French reverent (from Old French reverent) and its etymon Latin reverēns. By surface analysis, revere + -ent.
reverent.g: Showing or characterized by great respect or reverence; respectful.

reverse.e: From Middle English revers, from Anglo-Norman revers, Middle French revers, and their source, Latin reversus, perfect passive participle of reversō, from re- + versō.
reverse.g: Opposite, contrary; going in the opposite direction.

reverse.e: From Middle English reversen, from Anglo-Norman reverser, Middle French reverser, and their source, Latin reversō, from re- + versō.
reverse.g: To turn something around so that it faces the opposite direction or runs in the opposite sequence.

revert.e: From Old French revertir, from Vulgar Latin *revertiō, variant of Latin revertō.
revert.g: One who, or that which, reverts.

review.e: From Middle English revewe, reveue, from Old French reveüe, revue (Modern French: revue), feminine form of reveü, past participle of reveoir (French: revoir), from Latin revideō, from re- +videō (“see, observe”) (English: video). Equivalent to re- + view.
review.g: A second or subsequent reading of a text or artifact in an attempt to gain new insights.

revile.e: From Middle English revilen, from re + Old French aviler (“to make vile or cheap, disprize, disesteem”), from a- (“to”) + vil (“vile, cheap”); see vile.

revise.e: Borrowed from Middle French réviser, from Latin revīsō, from re- + vīsō (“examine”), frequentative of videō (“see”).
revise.g: To review, alter and amend, especially of written material.

revisit.e: From Middle English revisite, from Middle French revisiter and Latin revīsitāre. By surface analysis, re- + visit.

revoke.e: Borrowed from Middle French révoquer, from Latin revocare, from re- + voco, vocare.
revoke.g: To cancel or invalidate by withdrawing or reversing.

revolt.e: Borrowed from French révolter, from Italian rivoltare, itself either from ri- with the verb voltare, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *revoltāre < *revolvitāre, for *revolūtāre, frequentative of Latin revolvō (“roll back”) (through its past participle revolūtus).

revolter.g: Someone who revolts; a rebel or deserter

reward.e: From Middle English reward, rewarde, from Old French reward (“reward”) (compare Old French regard, whence modern French regard, and also English regard through Middle French), from rewarder (“to reward”) (compare Old French reguarder), from re- + warder (“to guard, keep”) (compare Old French guarder).
reward.g: Something of value given in return for an act.

reward.e: From Middle English rewarden, from Anglo-Norman rewarder (“to reward”), from re- + warder (“to guard, keep”), from Old Northern French, from Frankish *wardōn (“to guard, keep”), from Proto-Germanic *wardōną (“to guard, defend”), from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to cover, shelter, defend, guard, shut”). Piecewise doublet of regard.
reward.g: To give a reward to or for.
